opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today, while praying the Luminous Mysteries of the Rosary, I found myself praying for people. I prayed for family, clients, neighbors, people I see regularly but barely know. I sat quietly for a while, thinking about who else might need prayer.

And then some very different names came to mind. People I have very little respect for. People who have hurt me. People whose actions I have carried with me for a long time. There are even a few whom, if I am being truthful, I had allowed into what I might call my *“I hate them”* box. I don't use the word hate easily, but there are wounds that can harden us.

So I started saying their names. I didn't particularly enjoy it. With some names, I actually shuddered. Then another name would come to mind, and another. But something unexpected happened. I felt relief. It was almost as though, by praying for them, **I was allowing them to take the spear out of my heart.**

Later I read the Gospel in Matthew 18, where Peter asks Jesus, “Lord, if my brother sins against me, how often must I forgive him? As many as seven times?” Jesus answers, “I say to you, not seven times but seventy-seven times.”

I have read this Gospel many times. I knew what was coming. But today it landed differently. Jesus tells Peter the story of a servant who owes his master an enormous debt. The servant begs for mercy, and the master forgives the debt. Yet that same servant immediately finds someone who owes him far less and refuses to extend the mercy he has just received.

And suddenly I saw myself in the story. How many times have I asked God for mercy? How many times has He forgiven me? Yet I can still struggle to forgive the hurts caused by someone else—old hurts, new hurts, last week's hurts, yesterday's hurts, or even memories of something I thought I had already forgiven.

I began to understand why Jesus didn't simply tell Peter to forgive seven times. **Forgiveness isn't always something we do once.** I may genuinely forgive someone today and still remember the wound tomorrow. The anger may return. A memory may surface. Something may happen that opens the injury again. That doesn't necessarily mean the forgiveness wasn't real. It may mean I have to forgive again.

Maybe that is part of the seventy-seven times.

Forgiveness doesn't mean pretending something didn't happen. It doesn't mean saying that someone's actions were acceptable. It doesn't automatically restore trust, eliminate consequences, or require us to place ourselves back into situations where we can be hurt again. It means I no longer want to carry the debt.

And perhaps that is why praying for those people brought such relief. I wasn't changing what they had done. **I was asking God to change what their actions continued to do inside of me.**

There is another difficult part of Christian forgiveness: I cannot ask God to pour His mercy over my life while secretly hoping He withholds that mercy from someone else. The servant in Jesus' parable wanted mercy for himself and justice for everybody else. I understand that temptation. But Christ asks for something greater. He asks me to pray even for the person I would rather exclude, to place that person's name before God and allow God—not me—to determine what happens with their soul.

That doesn't excuse them. **It frees me.**

During the Rosary I also contemplated the Transfiguration. Jesus' glory was revealed to Peter, James, and John as He moved toward Jerusalem, where suffering and the Cross awaited Him. Before the disciples witnessed what would appear to be defeat, they were given a glimpse of who He truly was. Perhaps there is something here for us as well. Sometimes the road toward freedom passes directly through the thing we would rather avoid. Today, for me, that was forgiveness.

I don't know whether every wound I prayed about is completely healed. Probably not. But perhaps healing doesn't require me to pretend the hole isn't there. Perhaps every time that wound opens, I can ask God to fill it again—with His mercy, His strength, and eventually His peace.

And if tomorrow I remember the hurt again, I can forgive again. If it returns next week, again. If an old wound I thought was gone suddenly reappears, again.

Maybe seventy-seven times was never meant to be a number we could finally reach. Maybe Jesus was telling Peter something much more merciful:

**However many times the wound asks you to pick it back up, put it back into My hands.**
